#1
L: Him thus, by-pity-overcome, whose-eyes-were-tear-filled-and-troubled, despairing — this word Madhusūdana spoke.
I: Sañjaya said: To him — overcome with pity like this, his eyes filled with tears and troubled, sunk in despair — Madhusūdana spoke these words.
N: The chapter opens mid-scene: Kṛṣṇa, called here Madhusūdana ('slayer of Madhu'), answers Arjuna, whose collapse closed chapter 1. Kṛpayāviṣṭam is kṛpayā + āviṣṭam, 'entered by pity' — the same āviṣṭa- construction used of Arjuna's grief in 1.28 (kṛpayā parayāviṣṭaḥ); the grief named there is the target of Kṛṣṇa's first words here. Aśru-pūrṇa-ākula-īkṣaṇam is a bahuvrīhi (possessive compound): 'having eyes that are tear-filled and troubled'.
#2
L: Whence to-you this confusion, at-a-critical-moment come-upon — practiced-by-the-ignoble, not-leading-to-heaven, disgrace-causing, Arjuna?
I: The Blessed Lord said: Where has this weakness of yours come from at this critical moment, Arjuna? It is unworthy of a noble man, it leads to no heaven, and it brings only disgrace.
N: Kaśmala, 'taint, despondency', is a strong word — Kṛṣṇa treats Arjuna's collapse as a moral failure, not mere sensitivity. Three adjectives follow in a row, all built the same way: anārya-juṣṭam 'practiced by the ignoble' (an-ārya, someone without the values of a well-bred Ārya), asvargyam 'not leading to svarga (heaven)', akīrti-karam 'disgrace-making'. This is the first verse of Kṛṣṇa's teaching, which runs with only brief interruptions to the end of the poem.
#3
L: Unmanliness do not go-to, Pārtha; this in-you does not befit. Petty heart-weakness having-cast-off, arise, O scorcher-of-the-foe.
I: Do not give way to unmanliness, Pārtha — it does not become you. Cast off this petty faintheartedness and rise up, scorcher of the foe.
N: Mā gamaḥ, 'do not go [to]', is the aorist injunctive used with mā in prohibitions rather than the ordinary imperative — a construction that will recur through the poem. Klaibya, 'the state of a klība (an impotent man)', is a pointed insult to a warrior. Hṛdaya-daurbalyam, 'weakness of heart', is Kṛṣṇa's diagnosis of what chapter 1 showed; parantapa, 'scorcher of the foe', is an epithet elsewhere used of Arjuna himself.
#4
L: How Bhīṣma I in-battle, and Droṇa, with-arrows against shall-I-fight, O slayer-of-Madhu — the-two-worthy-of-honor, O slayer-of-foes?
I: Arjuna said: How can I meet Bhīṣma and Droṇa with arrows in battle, Madhusūdana? Both of them deserve my worship, slayer of enemies.
N: Arjuna answers with a question, not yet an argument — a rhetorical 'how?' (katham) that frames the whole speech running to verse 37. Pūjārhau, 'the two worthy of worship, of honor' (one dual adjective covering Bhīṣma and Droṇa together), states his real objection: these are not enemies to him but venerated elders. Ari-sūdana, 'slayer of foes', is one more epithet of Kṛṣṇa alongside Madhusūdana in the same verse — names of the god pile up even as Arjuna refuses violence.
#5
L: The-teachers not-having-killed, indeed, of-great-majesty — better it-is to-eat even alms-food here in-the-world; but the-teachers-desiring-gain having-killed, here indeed I-would-enjoy enjoyments blood-smeared.
I: Better to live here in this world on beggar's food, without killing these teachers of such greatness, than to enjoy, after killing them, pleasures smeared with the blood of teachers grown greedy for gain.
N: Gurūn, 'the teachers', covers both Bhīṣma and Droṇa; Arjuna argues that killing an elder poisons every pleasure that could follow, however compromised the elders' own motives (artha-kāmān, 'desiring wealth', hints that Bhīṣma and Droṇa fight for Duryodhana's cause, not conviction). Bhaikṣya, 'living on alms', is the diet of a renunciant who has given up the world — a striking alternative for a kṣatriya to name. The vulgate reads bhaikṣyam here; the BORI critical edition reads bhaikṣam instead, the same word without the -ya- suffix and with no difference of sense.
#6
L: And this we-do-not-know, which for-us [would-be] the-weightier — whether we-should-conquer, or if they-should-conquer us — those very ones, having-killed whom we-should-not-wish-to-live, stand-arrayed facing [us]: the-sons-of-Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
I: We do not even know which would be better for us — that we should conquer, or that we should be conquered. If we killed them, the very men now arrayed before us, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, we would not wish to go on living.
N: Yān eva hatvā na jijīviṣāmaḥ, 'those very men, having killed whom we should not wish to live' — Arjuna names his real fear for the first time: not death, but surviving the killing. The Wikisource text breaks the phrase jijīviṣāmas te 'vasthitāḥ oddly across a print line, splitting it into जिजीविषाम- and स्तेऽवस्थिताः; the two are one continuous phrase (jijīviṣāmaḥ + te + avasthitāḥ) and are drafted here as two words-entries only to tile the source exactly. Garīyaḥ, 'weightier, more important', is the comparative of guru — the same guru who is 'heavy' gives the ordinary word for 'teacher'.
#7
L: By-the-fault-of-weakness-afflicted-in-my-nature, I-ask you, whose-mind-is-confused-about-dharma: which [is] the-better — certain — tell that to-me. Your-pupil I [am]; instruct me, come-to-you-for-refuge.
I: My very nature is struck down by the weakness of pity, and my mind is confused about dharma; I ask you — tell me for certain what is truly better. I am your pupil: teach me, for I have come to you for refuge.
N: This is the pivot of the poem: Arjuna finally names what has happened to him (kārpaṇya, 'wretchedness, weakness of spirit', the noun behind klaibya in verse 3) and, unable to see his own dharma, formally asks to be taught. Śiṣyas te 'haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam, 'I am your pupil — teach me, who have come to you for refuge', is the moment Arjuna becomes a student rather than a friend giving orders; the rest of the poem answers this request. Prapanna, 'one who has taken refuge', returns at the house rendering of 18.66.
#8
L: For I-do-not-see-clearly what might-dispel this grief that-withers the-senses, even having-obtained on-earth an-unrivaled and-flourishing kingdom, or even overlordship of-the-gods.
I: I cannot see what could dispel this grief that is drying up my senses, even if I won a kingdom on earth, unrivaled and prosperous, or lordship over the gods themselves.
N: Arjuna's despair is stated here as total: no worldly prize, however great, could touch it — not even sovereignty over the gods (surāṇām ādhipatyam), the largest thing the epic imagination can name. This closes the question that Kṛṣṇa's teaching, beginning at verse 11, will answer — not by offering Arjuna a bigger prize, but by changing what grief and prize mean to him.
#9
L: Thus having-spoken to-the-Lord-of-the-senses, Guḍākeśa, O scorcher-of-the-foe: 'I will not fight' — thus, having-spoken to-Govinda, silent he-became, indeed.
I: Sañjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa said, O scorcher of the foe: 'I will not fight' — and having said this to Govinda, he fell silent.
N: The narrator's voice returns, and the whole speech from verse 4 closes on the flat declarative na yotsya iti, 'I will not fight'. Yotsya iti is a stock example of Sanskrit sandhi: the verb yotsye, ending in -e, is realized as yotsya before the quotation-marker iti. Parantapa here addresses Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as throughout the frame; Guḍākeśa and Hṛṣīkeśa are, as before, Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa.
#10
L: Him said Hṛṣīkeśa, smiling as-it-were, O Bhārata, between the-two-armies, to-the-one-despairing, this word.
I: Sañjaya said: To him, Hṛṣīkeśa, smiling as it were, spoke this word between the two armies, Bhārata, to Arjuna sunk in despair.
N: Prahasann iva, 'smiling, as it were', is the poem's only note of Kṛṣṇa's manner before he begins to teach; Śaṅkara reads the smile as amusement that a wise man's grief should be for the body, when the truth about to be stated is that the self cannot die. Senayor ubhayor madhye, 'between the two armies', repeats 1.21 verbatim, closing the frame opened there.
#11
L: For-those-not-to-be-grieved-for you-grieved, and words-of-wisdom you-speak; for-those-whose-breath-has-gone and-for-those-whose-breath-has-not-gone the-wise do-not-grieve.
I: The Blessed Lord said: You grieve for those not to be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.
N: Kṛṣṇa's teaching begins with a paradox stated in one line: Arjuna talks like a paṇḍita (a learned man) while acting like a fool, grieving for men who do not deserve grief. Gatāsūn agatāsūn, 'those whose breath has gone' and 'those whose breath has not gone' — the dead and the living — is the first hint of the argument to come: that the distinction between dead and alive is not, at the deepest level, the one that matters. This opens the section on the immortality of the self that runs to verse 30.
#12
L: For never indeed I did-not-exist, nor you, nor these lords-of-men; nor indeed shall-we-not-be, all of-us, hereafter.
I: There was never a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings; nor will there ever be a time hereafter when any of us ceases to be.
N: The first positive claim of the teaching: not merely that the self does not die in this one death, but that it has always existed and always will — na tv evāhaṃ jātu nāsam, 'for indeed I never did not exist'. Kṛṣṇa speaks of himself, Arjuna, and 'these kings' (janādhipāḥ, the assembled warriors) all in the same breath, as if from outside time looking at the whole scene at once — a first glimpse of the more explicit divine claim that comes only in chapter 4 and after.
#13
L: Of-the-embodied-one, in-this body, as [there is] childhood, youth, old-age, so [there is] the-attaining-of-another-body; the-steady-one there does-not-become-confused.
I: Just as the embodied self passes, in this body, through childhood, youth and old age, so too it passes into another body; the wise man is not confused by this.
N: The argument's central image: the self (dehin, 'the embodied one', the ātman as it possesses a body) already changes bodies constantly within one lifetime — child to youth to old man — so passing into a wholly different body at death (dehāntara-prāpti) is nothing new in kind, only in degree. Dhīra, 'steady, resolute', becomes one of the poem's recurring words for the man who is not shaken (compare verse 15, and muni at verse 56). This is the first statement of what later tradition calls reincarnation, argued here purely by analogy with the body's own changes.
#14
L: The-sense-contacts, indeed, O son-of-Kuntī, giving-cold-and-heat-and-pleasure-and-pain, coming-and-going, impermanent — them endure, O Bhārata.
I: The contacts of the senses with their objects, Kaunteya, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go; they are impermanent. Endure them, Bhārata.
N: Mātrā-sparśāḥ, 'sense-contacts' (mātrā here in the old sense of an element or measure of experience), names what both chapter 1's symptoms of shock and chapter 2's grief are: sensations, arising from contact between sense and object, that come and go like weather. Āgamāpāyinaḥ, 'coming and going', a bahuvrīhi, states their nature directly; titikṣasva, 'endure them', is the practical instruction that follows from that nature, before the metaphysical argument about the self resumes in the next verse.
#15
L: Whom indeed these [sense-contacts] do-not-disturb, [that] man, O bull-among-men, to-whom-pain-and-pleasure-are-equal, steady — he for-immortality becomes-fit.
I: The man whom these sensations do not disturb, bull among men, who is unmoved alike by pleasure and pain, steady — he is fit for immortality.
N: Amṛtatva, 'the state of amṛta, deathlessness', names for the first time the goal the whole teaching aims at; kalpate, 'is fit for, is equal to [the task of]', treats immortality as something to be qualified for by a settled character, not simply granted. Sama-duḥkha-sukham, 'to whom pain and pleasure are equal', is a compound that recurs almost verbatim later in the poem and becomes a name for equanimity itself.
#16
L: Of-the-non-existent there-is-found no coming-to-be; of-the-existent there-is-found no ceasing-to-be; of-both indeed, seen [is] the-conclusion, of-these-two, by-the-seers-of-truth.
I: Of the unreal there is no being; of the real there is no non-being. This conclusion, about both, has been seen by the seers of truth.
N: The famous line that grounds the whole argument: bhāva and abhāva ('coming to be' and 'not being') simply cannot apply to asat and sat (the unreal and the real) respectively — what is real cannot stop being real, and what is unreal never was real to begin with. The second half names the source of this claim directly: tattva-darśibhiḥ, 'by the seers of the truth' — not Kṛṣṇa's private opinion, but what those who see reality as it is have always seen (dṛṣṭo 'ntaḥ, 'the conclusion has been seen').
#17
L: Indestructible, but, that know — by-which all this [world is] pervaded; the-destruction of-this imperishable-one no-one is-able to-bring-about.
I: But know that to be indestructible, by which all this is pervaded; no one can bring about the destruction of this imperishable thing.
N: Tat, 'that', is the first naming — still unnamed as ātman — of the reality behind everything: whatever pervades (tatam, from the same root as the ordinary word for a thread or web) the whole visible world is what cannot be destroyed. Na kaścit kartum arhati, 'no one is able to bring it about', restates verse 16's dṛṣṭo 'ntaḥ as a flat impossibility, just before the poem's most systematic listing of the self's indestructibility begins at verse 18. The same root tan returns in the metaphor of 7.7, where all things are said to be strung on Kṛṣṇa like jewels on a thread.
#18
L: Having-an-end [are] these bodies, of-the-eternal called, of-the-embodied-one — of-the-imperishable, of-the-immeasurable; therefore fight, O Bhārata.
I: These bodies are said to have an end, but the embodied self that dwells in them is eternal, imperishable, immeasurable. Therefore fight, Bhārata.
N: The verse states the whole distinction the argument has been building toward: dehāḥ, 'bodies', are antavantaḥ, 'finite, ending'; the śarīrin/dehin who wears them is nitya, 'eternal', anāśin, 'undying', aprameya, 'immeasurable, beyond the reach of proof'. Tasmād yudhyasva, 'therefore fight', is the first time the command to fight is grounded explicitly in this metaphysics, rather than simply asserted as in verse 3.
#19
L: Who him knows [as] the-slayer, and-who him thinks [to-be] slain — both-of-them do-not-understand: this-one does-not-kill, nor is-killed.
I: He who thinks this self a killer, and he who thinks it killed, both fail to understand: it does not kill, nor is it killed.
N: The famous couplet nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate, 'this [self] neither kills nor is killed', is quoted independently across Indian tradition; it answers, for the first time explicitly, the fear Arjuna raised in verse 4 (how can I kill Bhīṣma and Droṇa?) by denying that killing, in the relevant sense, ever touches the self at all — only the body. Hantāram, 'the slayer', and hatam, 'the slain', are exactly the two false views the verse rejects together.
#20
L: It-is-not-born, nor does-it-die ever; nor, having-come-to-be, will-it ever-again cease-to-be — unborn, eternal, everlasting, this ancient one; it-is-not-killed when-the-body-is-being-killed.
I: It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come to be, it will never again cease to be. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.
N: This verse states the self's unbornness and deathlessness as flatly as possible, in two parallel halves: na jāyate mriyate vā, then a run of four synonyms — ajaḥ, nityaḥ, śāśvataḥ, purāṇaḥ ('unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient') — for the same claim. The middle clause, na ayaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ, is the hardest to parse literally: 'nor, having come to be, will it cease to be again' — denying that the self even has the ordinary kind of existence that begins and could later end. This verse and the one before are cited independently across the tradition, and appear, essentially unchanged, at Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18.
#21
L: Him-who-knows [as] indestructible, eternal, unborn, undecaying — who, that man, O Pārtha, how does-he-cause-to-be-killed whom, [or] kill whom?
I: How, Pārtha, can the man who knows this self to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and undecaying, cause anyone to be killed, or kill anyone himself?
N: The verse draws the practical conclusion from verses 19–20: if the self cannot be killed, a man who truly knows this (veda, a perfect used as a simple present, 'knows') cannot, in the relevant sense, be a killer at all — kaṃ ghātayati hanti kam, 'whom does he cause to be killed, [or] kill whom?', repeating kam for emphasis. Ghātayati, the causative of han, covers ordering or causing a killing as distinct from doing it directly; both are denied of the man of knowledge.
#22
L: As garments, worn-out, having-cast-off, new ones a-man takes, other [ones]; so bodies, worn-out and-other, having-cast-off, passes-into new [ones] the-embodied-one.
I: Just as a man casts off worn-out garments and takes other, new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and passes into others that are new.
N: The chapter's most famous simile: the self changes bodies at death the way a person changes clothes — an image that returns the argument to the everyday after several verses of abstract metaphysics. Vāsāṃsi ('garments') and śarīrāṇi ('bodies') are matched term for term across the two half-lines, down to jīrṇāni ('worn out') and navāni ('new') repeated in both.
#23
L: This-one weapons do-not-cut, this-one fire does-not-burn; and-this-one waters do-not-wet, [nor] wind dries-it.
I: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, nor does wind dry it.
N: The four elements each get their own verb and their own failure: chid ('cut') for weapons, dah ('burn') for fire, klid ('wet') for water, śuṣ ('dry') for wind — a rhetorical exhaustion of every physical way something could be destroyed, each denied of the self in turn.
#24
L: Uncuttable this, unburnable this, unwettable, undryable indeed and; eternal, all-pervading, fixed, unmoving this, everlasting.
I: This self cannot be cut, burnt, wetted or dried; it is eternal, all-pervading, fixed, unmoving, everlasting.
N: The four negative gerundives (acchedya, adāhya, akledya, aśoṣya) restate verse 23's four elements as fixed attributes; five more epithets follow in the second line — the pile-up of near-synonyms (nitya, sanātana both 'eternal'; sthāṇu, acala both 'unmoving') is itself the rhetorical point: no single word is adequate, so the verse surrounds the self with as many as it can find.
#25
L: Unmanifest this, unthinkable this, unchangeable this, it-is-called; therefore, thus, having-known-it, not to-grieve-for-it you-ought.
I: This self is called unmanifest, unthinkable, unchangeable. Knowing it to be so, you ought not to grieve.
N: Avyakta ('unmanifest'), acintya ('beyond thought') and avikārya ('unchangeable') push the description past the physical (verses 23–24) to declare the self beyond perception and even beyond conceptual grasp — a step that anticipates the language later used of brahman. The refrain nānuśocitum arhasi, 'you ought not to grieve', closes the argument opened at verse 11 and recurs, with small variations, through verse 30.
#26
L: But if, also, this-one [as] constantly-born or constantly dead you-think — even-so, you, O mighty-armed-one, thus you-ought-not to-grieve.
I: But even if you think of this self as constantly being born and constantly dying, even so, mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve like this.
N: Kṛṣṇa now argues from the opposite premise, as a fallback: even granting the ordinary view that the self is born and dies again and again (nitya-jātaṃ nityaṃ vā mṛtam — transmigration understood as brute recurring birth-and-death, rather than the deathless self of verses 19–25), grief is still unwarranted, because birth makes death certain and death makes rebirth certain, as the next verse goes on to say. The vulgate reads naivaṃ, 'not thus, not in this way', in the second line; the BORI critical edition reads nainaṃ (na + enam, 'should not grieve for it') in its place, which shifts what is denied from the manner of grieving to the self itself — a small but real difference in what the line says.
#27
L: Of-the-born, indeed, certain [is] death; certain [is] birth of-the-dead, and; therefore, in-a-matter-unavoidable, not you ought to-grieve.
I: For the one who is born, death is certain; and for the one who dies, birth is certain. Therefore you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.
N: A tightly reasoned couplet in the strict logical style the poem uses when closing an argument: birth entails death, death (on this view of recurring transmigration) entails birth, so the whole cycle is aparihārya, 'unavoidable' — as fixed as any law of nature, and no more fit an object for grief than winter following autumn.
#28
L: Unmanifest-in-their-beginning [are] beings, manifest-in-their-middle, O Bhārata, unmanifest-in-their-end indeed; there what [room for] lamentation?
I: Beings are unmanifest before birth, manifest between birth and death, and unmanifest again after death, Bhārata. What is there in that to lament?
N: A third argument, from ordinary experience rather than metaphysics: whatever a being is before birth and after death is already unmanifest and unknown to us, and only the interval between (vyakta-madhya, 'manifest in the middle') is visible — so death returns a being to a state no stranger than the one it came from, and no more a cause for grief.
#29
L: As-a-wonder someone sees it, and-as-a-wonder someone-else speaks-of it, likewise; and-as-a-wonder another hears it; and-even having-heard, no-one at-all knows it.
I: One looks on this self as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; yet even having heard, no one truly knows it.
N: A verse built almost entirely from the one word āścaryavat, 'as a wonder, wonderingly', repeated for the seer, the speaker and the hearer alike; the final clause, śrutvāpy enaṃ veda na caiva kaścit, 'even having heard, no one at all knows it', admits, within the teaching itself, that the self it describes exceeds ordinary knowing — a note of humility rare in the chapter's otherwise confident argument.
#30
L: The-embodied-one always inviolable this, in-the-body of-everyone, O Bhārata; therefore, for-all beings, not you ought to-grieve.
I: This embodied self, Bhārata, is always inviolable in everyone's body. Therefore you ought not to grieve for any being.
N: The section that began at verse 11 closes exactly where it started, restating nānuśocitum arhasi ('you ought not to grieve') one last time, now generalized from Bhīṣma and Droṇa to sarvāṇi bhūtāni, 'all beings' — the argument was never really only about this one battle. Verse 31 turns from what the self is to what Arjuna, as a kṣatriya, must do regardless.
#31
L: One's-own-dharma also, having-considered, not you-ought to-waver; for than-a-righteous battle, better other-thing for-a-kṣatriya not there-is-found.
I: And considering your own dharma too, you should not waver: for a kṣatriya, there is nothing better than a righteous war.
N: A second, entirely separate argument now begins, running to verse 38: not the metaphysics of the self, but Arjuna's sva-dharma, 'own dharma', kept untranslated per convention — the duty specific to his class and station. Dharmya, 'righteous, lawful', names this particular war as one fought for a just cause (to recover the Pāṇḍavas' kingdom), which is what makes the argument work: not every war would qualify.
#32
L: By-chance and come, the-gate-of-heaven thrown-open; happy [are the] kṣatriyas, O Pārtha, [who] obtain a-battle such-as-this.
I: Happy are the kṣatriyas, Pārtha, who find, by sheer chance, a war like this — an open gate to heaven.
N: Yadṛcchayā copapannam, 'come about by mere chance', marks that this battle is not something Arjuna sought out — refusing it means throwing away, rather than merely declining, an opportunity that came unbidden. Svarga-dvāram apāvṛtam, 'the gate of heaven flung open', names the reward Vedic tradition offers a kṣatriya who dies fighting justly — a promise the poem will later, from verse 42 on, treat with some suspicion when it becomes the object of desire.
#33
L: But if you this righteous battle will-not do, then, one's-own-dharma and fame, having-abandoned, sin you-will-incur.
I: But if you will not fight this righteous battle, then, having abandoned your own dharma and your fame, you will incur sin.
N: The consequence side of the sva-dharma argument: refusing this particular fight is not neutral but an active abandonment (hitvā) of both dharma and kīrti, 'fame' — a warrior's two chief goods — incurring pāpa, 'sin, evil', in their place. The next three verses spell out exactly what form that lost fame and incurred sin will take among people who hear of Arjuna's refusal.
#34
L: Disgrace, and-also, [about-you] people will-tell, undying; and-of-one-honored disgrace than-death exceeds.
I: People will speak forever of your disgrace, and for a man once honored, disgrace is worse than death.
N: Akīrtim ... avyayām, 'disgrace ... undying', frames Arjuna's shame as a terrible immortality of its own, set against the true immortality of the self just taught in verses 12–30 — a bitter irony the verse leaves for the reader to notice. Saṃbhāvita, 'one held in high regard' (a causative past participle of bhū, 'to esteem'), is precisely Arjuna's own standing among his peers, which the argument says he is about to forfeit.
#35
L: Out-of-fear from-battle withdrawn they-will-think you, the-great-chariot-warriors; and-of-whom, you, highly-esteemed having-been, you-will-go [to] contempt.
I: The great warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear, and you will fall into contempt among those who once held you in high regard.
N: A social argument continues from verse 34: it is not fear itself but the appearance of fear, in the eyes of the very men Arjuna cares most about (mahārathāḥ, the great warriors of both armies), that the verse names as the real cost. Bahumato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam, 'having been highly esteemed, you will go into contempt', measures the fall precisely by the height of Arjuna's present reputation.
#36
L: Unspeakable-words many they-will-speak, your ill-wishers, reviling your capability; than-that more-painful, then, what?
I: Your enemies will say many unspeakable things about you, mocking your ability; and what could be more painful than that?
N: Ahitāḥ, 'those without goodwill', is a euphemism for enemies proper; the verse imagines the Kauravas mocking Arjuna's sāmarthya, 'capability, prowess' — the one thing a kṣatriya's whole identity rests on. Duḥkhataraṃ nu kim, 'what could be more painful?', closes the social argument on its strongest note before the summary in verse 37.
#37
L: Slain, or, you-will-attain heaven; or, having-conquered, you-will-enjoy the-earth; therefore arise, O son-of-Kuntī, for-battle with-resolve-made.
I: If killed, you will attain heaven; if victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore rise up, Kaunteya, resolved to fight.
N: The social argument closes on a claim that leaves Arjuna no losing option at all: slain, he wins heaven; victorious, he wins the earth. Kṛta-niścayaḥ, 'with his resolve made', anticipates the technical sense of niścaya (firm resolve) that the coming section on buddhi will build on.
#38
L: Pleasure-and-pain equal having-made, gain-and-loss, victory-and-defeat, then for-battle engage; thus sin you-will-not-incur.
I: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, engage in battle; in this way you will not incur sin.
N: The first appearance of the equanimity this poem calls samatva ('the state of being equal, evenness'), applied here directly to the outcomes of battle: three pairs (sukha-duḥkhe, lābhālābhau, jayājayau) that together cover everything at stake. Verse 38 is a hinge: it still argues from the fruits of action, as verses 32–37 did, but its method — meeting every outcome with an equal mind — is exactly what verses 39–53 turn into a discipline in its own right, what later tradition calls niṣkāma karma, 'action without craving for its fruit', though that phrase itself is not the poem's own.
#39
L: This to-you has-been-declared in-Sāṃkhya, the-understanding; but this in-yoga hear — by-which understanding yoked, O Pārtha, the-bondage-of-action you-will-cast-off.
I: This is the understanding declared to you in Sāṃkhya; now hear it in yoga, disciplined by which you will cast off the bondage of action, Pārtha.
N: A hinge verse naming, for the first time, the two approaches the poem keeps returning to: Sāṃkhya, the analysis just given (verses 11–38, distinguishing self from body, duty from desire), and yoga, the discipline of acting that Kṛṣṇa now turns to teach — not two rival philosophies but two ways into the same understanding. Sāṃkhya is treated here as a proper name, alongside yoga, and left untranslated in both by analogy with the convention for yoga, though conventions.md names only yoga, dharma, brahman and the guṇas explicitly — flagged for review. Buddhi, 'discernment, judgment, resolve', becomes the chapter's central word from here to verse 53 and returns, transformed, in the description of the sthitaprajña beginning at verse 54.
#40
L: Here of-undertaking-loss there-is-not; adverse-result not there-is-found; even-a-little of-this dharma protects from-great danger.
I: In this discipline no effort is ever lost, and no harm is ever done; even a little of this dharma protects one from great danger.
N: Iha, 'here', points back to the yoga just named in verse 39: unlike an ordinary ritual act, wasted (abhikrama-nāśa) if not completed correctly, an act done in this spirit has value even incomplete, since its value lies in the doing rather than in a specific external result.
#41
L: Of-the-nature-of-firm-resolve, [is] the-understanding, single, here, O joy-of-the-Kurus; but many-branched and-endless [are] the-understandings of-those-without-firm-resolve.
I: In this discipline the resolve is single and firmly fixed, joy of the Kurus; but the thoughts of the irresolute branch out endlessly.
N: Ekā, 'single, one', against bahuśākhāḥ ... anantāḥ, 'many-branched and endless': the man of yoga has one settled buddhi (here closer to 'resolve' than 'intellect'), while the irresolute (avyavasāyinām) scatter their attention across countless competing aims — a contrast the next three verses illustrate with the ritualists who chase heaven through many rites rather than fixing on one thing.
#42
L: This flowery speech which they-proclaim, the-undiscerning, devoted-to-the-doctrine-of-the-Veda, O Pārtha, [saying] 'there-is nothing-else', thus declaring —
I: The undiscerning, Pārtha, who delight in the flowery language of the Vedic ritualists and declare that there is nothing beyond it —
N: The sentence beginning here runs through verse 44, a long period typical of the poem's more argumentative stretches. Puṣpitāṃ vācam, 'flowery speech', is a pointed image: attractive, ornamented language that promises much while, the poem argues, missing the point. Veda-vāda-ratāḥ, 'devoted to the ritual doctrine of the Veda', targets not the Veda itself but a narrow, literalist reading of its ritual portion as though rites for heaven were the whole of it; Kṛṣṇa's own relation to the Veda is addressed again at verses 45–46.
#43
L: Whose-nature-is-desire, having-heaven-as-their-highest-aim, [speech] giving-good-birth-as-the-fruit-of-action, full-of-various-particular-rites, toward the-attainment-of-enjoyment-and-power —
I: — men whose nature is desire, who look on heaven as their highest goal, who offer speech promising rebirth as the fruit of ritual action, and are full of specific rites aimed only at pleasure and power —
N: The sentence continues without its own finite verb, piling description onto the veda-vāda-ratāḥ of verse 42: kāma-ātmānaḥ, 'whose very self is desire', svarga-parāḥ, 'for whom heaven is the highest thing'. The critique is not of ritual as such but of ritual performed for these narrower ends (enjoyment, power, a better rebirth) rather than as an offering without expectation of return — the positive alternative verse 47 goes on to state.
#44
L: Of-those-attached-to-enjoyment-and-power, by-that [speech] whose-minds-are-carried-away — the-resolve-of-firm-nature in-concentration is-not established.
I: For men attached to enjoyment and power, their minds carried away by such talk, no firmly settled resolve is ever formed in concentration.
N: The long sentence from verse 42 finally reaches its main clause: for such men, no vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ ('single, firmly resolved understanding', the very thing praised in verse 41) can form in samādhi, 'a settled, concentrated mind' — the ritualists' scattered aims of verses 42–43 are the direct cause of the scattered buddhi verse 41 already criticized.
#45
L: Having-the-three-guṇas-as-their-domain [are] the-Vedas; free-from-the-three-guṇas be, Arjuna — free-from-the-pairs-of-opposites, ever-grounded-in-sattva, without-concern-for-gain-and-keeping, self-possessed.
I: The Vedas deal with the domain of the three guṇas; be free of the three guṇas, Arjuna — free from the pairs of opposites, ever grounded in sattva, unconcerned with gain and security, master of yourself.
N: Guṇa (compounded here as trai-guṇya, 'the domain of the three guṇas') is left untranslated per convention, even though the poem does not name the three guṇas individually until chapter 14; here it means simply the whole domain of ordinary nature's conditions, of which sattva (also left untranslated as guṇa-vocabulary) is one. Nistraiguṇyaḥ, 'beyond the three guṇas', states more directly than before that the goal lies past the whole system Vedic ritual operates within, not merely past bad ritual. Yoga-kṣema, 'acquiring and keeping safe' — the getting and the guarding of possessions — has a long later life in Indian religious and economic vocabulary alike; freedom from concern for either marks the self-possessed (ātmavān) man.
#46
L: As-much use [as there is] in-a-well, on-all-sides in-a-flood-of-water, so-much [use is there] in-all the-Vedas, for-a-brahmin who-understands.
I: As much use as there is in a well when water is flooding on every side, so much is the use of all the Vedas to a brahmin who understands.
N: A simile that qualifies, without rejecting, the Veda's value: once the whole country is under flood, a single well adds nothing — likewise, for the man who has reached the understanding just described, the Vedas add nothing beyond what he already has, though they were of real use to him before he arrived there. Vijānataḥ brāhmaṇasya, 'for a brahmin who understands', is the positive counterpart to the merely ritual brahmins criticized in verses 42–44.
#47
L: In action alone is your entitlement, never in its fruits; do not let the fruit of action be your motive, and let there be no attachment of yours to inaction.
I: Your claim is to the action itself, never to what comes of it. Do not act for the sake of results, and do not cling to not acting either.
N: The most quoted verse of the poem, and the summary of the teaching on action running through verses 38–53. Adhikāra, 'entitlement, the right or standing [to do something]', is a term from ritual law: one is qualified to perform a rite and claim its fruit, but Kṛṣṇa restricts the adhikāra itself to the doing, never the phala, 'fruit'. Mā karma-phala-hetur bhūḥ uses the aorist injunctive with mā (as already at verse 3, mā ... gamaḥ) for a sharp prohibition: 'never let the fruit of action be your motive'. The final clause guards against a possible misreading of everything just said — that if the fruit does not matter, one might as well stop acting — by forbidding attachment to akarman, 'inaction', just as firmly as attachment to the fruit; this concern is taken up at length in chapter 3.
#48
L: Grounded-in-yoga, do actions, attachment having-abandoned, O Dhanaṃjaya; in-success-and-failure equal having-become — evenness [is what] yoga is-called.
I: Perform actions grounded in yoga, Dhanaṃjaya, having abandoned attachment, even-minded alike in success and failure — for evenness of mind is what is meant by yoga.
N: The chapter's one explicit definition of yoga (kept untranslated, as the technical term the poem is here naming): samatvaṃ yoga ucyate, 'evenness [of mind] is called yoga'. Siddhy-asiddhyoḥ, 'in success and failure', restates the three pairs of verse 38 as a single pair covering any outcome at all; yoga-sthaḥ, 'standing in yoga', frames the whole verse as instruction for how to act, not whether to.
#49
L: By-far, indeed, inferior [is] action than-the-yoga-of-understanding, O Dhanaṃjaya; in-understanding refuge seek — wretched [are those] motivated-by-the-fruit.
I: Action by itself is far inferior to the yoga of understanding, Dhanaṃjaya; seek refuge in understanding — pitiable are those who act for the fruit.
N: Buddhi-yoga, 'the yoga of understanding' (naming the whole discipline taught since verse 39), is here set explicitly above ordinary action performed with an eye to its fruit; kṛpaṇāḥ, 'wretched, pitiable' — the same root behind Arjuna's own kārpaṇya, 'weakness of spirit', at verse 7 — brands the fruit-seeker with the very word Arjuna used of his own collapse.
#50
L: Joined-to-understanding, one-abandons here [both] merit-and-demerit; therefore for-yoga engage — yoga [is] skill in-actions.
I: One who is joined to understanding leaves behind, in this very life, both merit and demerit. Therefore engage yourself in yoga — yoga is skill in action.
N: A second definition of yoga, as famous as verse 48's: yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam, 'yoga is skill in actions'. Sukṛta-duṣkṛte, 'merit and demerit', are the two kinds of result an ordinary ritual act accumulates; the buddhi-yukta, 'one joined to understanding', leaves both behind iha, 'right here, in this life', rather than only after death — the discipline pays off immediately, not merely in some future rebirth.
#51
L: The-fruit-born-of-action, joined-to-understanding, indeed, having-abandoned, the-wise; freed-from-the-bondage-of-birth, to-the-place they-go untroubled.
I: The wise, joined to understanding, abandon the fruit born of action; freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the place beyond all trouble.
N: Padam ... anāmayam, 'the untroubled place', is one of the poem's early names for the goal itself, before it acquires more developed names later, such as brahman; janma-bandha, 'the bondage of birth [and rebirth]', is the condition the whole discipline is meant to release one from, stated here for the first time in so many words.
#52
L: When your the-tangle-of-delusion the-understanding will-cross-beyond, then you-will-attain indifference toward-what-is-to-be-heard and-what-has-been-heard.
I: When your understanding has crossed beyond the tangle of delusion, you will become indifferent to all that has been heard and all that is yet to be heard.
N: Śrotavyasya śrutasya ca, 'of what is to be heard and what has been heard', points at scriptural teaching generally, recalling the ritualists of verses 42–44; nirveda, 'disenchantment, indifference', names not apathy but the state of no longer needing to hear any more — the same relation to the Vedas already stated by the well-and-flood simile of verse 46.
#53
L: Confused-by-scripture your, when it-will-stand unwavering; in-concentration unmoving, the-understanding, then yoga you-will-attain.
I: When your understanding, now confused by conflicting scripture, stands unwavering and unmoving in concentration, then you will attain yoga.
N: This closes the buddhi-yoga section begun at verse 39: the buddhi that was scattered by the many-branched claims of ritual scripture (śruti-vipratipannā, 'distracted by what is heard', echoing verses 41–44) finally becomes acalā, 'unmoving', in samādhi — the very state denied in verse 44 (buddhiḥ ... na vidhīyate) now affirmed. Yogam avāpsyasi, 'you will attain yoga', answers Arjuna's opening request (verse 7, 'tell me what is truly better') in the discipline's own terms, before the dialogue turns, at verse 54, to what such a man of settled understanding actually looks like.
#54
L: Of-one-whose-wisdom-is-steady, what [is the] manner-of-speech, of-one-situated-in-concentration, O Keśava? [One] of-steady-mind, how would-he-speak, how would-he-abide, would-he-walk how?
I: Arjuna said: What is the mark of a man whose wisdom is steady, who is settled in concentration, Keśava? How would such a man of steady mind speak, how would he sit, how would he walk?
N: After the long teaching on buddhi-yoga (verses 39–53), Arjuna asks a very practical question: what does such a man actually look like? Sthita-prajña, 'one whose wisdom stands firm', becomes the technical name (introduced here and defined at verse 55) for the portrait that fills the rest of the chapter. The three verbs — speak, sit, walk — ask about speech, stillness and motion in turn, and Kṛṣṇa's answer moves through all three.
#55
L: When he-abandons-completely all desires present-in-the-mind, O Pārtha, in-the-self alone by-the-self content — [he] one-whose-wisdom-is-steady then is-called.
I: The Blessed Lord said: When a man gives up completely all the desires that have entered his mind, Pārtha, content in the self alone by the self, he is then called one of steady wisdom.
N: The defining verse for sthita-prajña, answering Arjuna's question with a definition before the description proper begins: kāmān ... prajahāti, 'he abandons desires', and ātmani eva ātmanā tuṣṭaḥ, 'content in the self alone by the self', without an external object — a self-sufficiency that returns in different words through verses 56–71.
#56
L: Whose-mind-is-unperturbed in-sorrows, in-pleasures from-whom-craving-has-departed, free-from-passion-fear-and-anger — [he] the-steady-minded, a-sage, is-called.
I: One whose mind is not disturbed by sorrows and does not crave pleasures, who is free from passion, fear and anger — such a man is called a sage of steady mind.
N: The portrait continues with pairs answering how the sthita-prajña relates to duḥkha and sukha (echoing sama-duḥkha-sukham at verse 15): unmoved by suffering, uncraving of pleasure. Muni, 'a sage, a silent one' (from man, 'to think', but traditionally associated with silence), gives the sthitaprajña a second name, alongside dhīra (verses 13, 15), in this poem's family of words for the man of settled mind.
#57
L: Who everywhere without-attachment, this-or-that having-obtained, good-or-bad, does-not-rejoice, does-not-hate — his wisdom [is] firmly-established.
I: He who is everywhere without attachment, on meeting with anything good or bad, neither rejoices nor hates — his wisdom is firmly established.
N: A general principle stated for the first time here: attachment (sneha) itself, not the specific quality of the outcome, is what has to go — the sthitaprajña meets good and bad alike, not because he cannot tell them apart but because he holds neither. Prajñā pratiṣṭhitā, 'wisdom firmly established', becomes a refrain closing several of the following verses (58, 61, 68), each time restating that the wisdom asked about at verse 54 rests on a different specific practice.
#58
L: When he-draws-in, and this-one, [his] limbs, as-a-tortoise, wholly, the-senses from-the-objects-of-the-senses — his wisdom [is] firmly-established.
I: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs from every side, he withdraws his senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly established.
N: The famous tortoise simile — kūrmo 'ṅgānīva sarvaśaḥ, 'like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side' — gives sense-withdrawal a single memorable image; the refrain prajñā pratiṣṭhitā closes the verse as it did verse 57.
#59
L: The-sense-objects turn-away from-the-embodied-one who-abstains, except relish; even the-relish of-him, the-supreme having-seen, turns-back.
I: For one who abstains, the objects of the senses fall away, except the relish for them; but even that relish falls away once he has seen the supreme.
N: A qualification of verse 58's tortoise image: mere abstention (nirāhāra) removes the objects but can leave rasa, 'the relish, the taste for them', lingering underneath — full freedom comes only when even that relish drops away, and only on seeing param, 'the supreme'. This is the first hint in the sthitaprajña section that the discipline rests on a positive vision, not just self-control.
#60
L: Of-one-who-strives, indeed, even, O son-of-Kuntī, of-a-man discerning — the-senses, turbulent, carry-off forcibly the-mind.
I: For even the man of discernment who is striving hard, Kaunteya, the turbulent senses can forcibly carry off his mind.
N: A candid warning right after two verses that might sound reassuring: even the vipaścit, 'discerning man', who is actively yatataḥ, 'striving', is not safe — the indriyāṇi pramāthīni, 'turbulent senses', can overpower the mind by force (prasabham). This sets up the practical instruction of the next verse.
#61
L: Them, all, having-restrained, disciplined he-should-remain, intent-on-me; for whose senses [are] in-control, his wisdom [is] firmly-established.
I: Having restrained them all, he should remain disciplined, intent on me; for the man whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established.
N: The instruction following directly from verse 60's warning: saṃyamya, 'having restrained', is the practical remedy for the senses' pull. Mat-paraḥ, 'intent on me [Kṛṣṇa]', is the poem's first direct call to fix one's attention on Kṛṣṇa personally, rather than only on the impersonal ātman or buddhi described so far — a note that becomes central only much later, from chapter 7 on.
#62
L: Of-one-dwelling-upon sense-objects, of-a-man, attachment to-them arises; from-attachment is-born desire, from-desire anger arises.
I: When a man dwells on sense-objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment desire is born, and from desire anger arises.
N: The first links of a chain of causation running through this verse and the next — dhyāna (dwelling on an object) leads to saṅga (attachment), then kāma (desire), then krodha (anger) — each explicitly said to arise (jāyate, with various prefixes) from the one before, in the poem's clearest statement of exactly how a mind loses its footing.
#63
L: From-anger arises confusion, from-confusion loss-of-memory; from-loss-of-memory [comes] ruin-of-understanding, from-ruin-of-understanding he-perishes.
I: From anger comes confusion, from confusion the loss of memory; from loss of memory, the ruin of understanding, and from the ruin of understanding, a man is lost.
N: The chain from verse 62 completes itself: krodha, then saṃmoha, smṛti-vibhrama, buddhi-nāśa, and finally praṇaśyati, 'he perishes utterly' — each step named by the same jāyate/bhavati family of verbs, so that verses 62–63 read as a single mechanism rather than an abstract moral warning. Buddhi-nāśa, 'the ruin of understanding', is the exact opposite of the vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ prized since verse 41; the two verses trace, cause by cause, how one turns into the other.
#64
L: But with-senses-freed-from-passion-and-aversion moving-among sense-objects, [his senses] brought-under-the-self's-control, one-whose-self-is-disciplined, attains tranquility.
I: But the disciplined man, moving among sense-objects with his senses freed from passion and aversion and under the control of his own self, attains tranquility.
N: Answering the danger of verses 60–63 without demanding total withdrawal from sense-objects (which verse 59 already showed to be insufficient by itself): the man who moves among objects rāga-dveṣa-viyuktaiḥ, 'with passion and aversion set aside', is safe precisely because it is the passion and aversion, not contact with the world itself, that starts the chain of ruin. Prasāda, 'clarity, tranquility' (also 'grace'), names the positive state that follows once that danger is removed, and becomes the pivot word of the next verse.
#65
L: In-tranquility, of-all-sorrows the-cessation, of-him, arises; for of-one-of-tranquil-mind, quickly, the-understanding becomes-firmly-settled.
I: In that tranquility, all his sorrows come to an end; for the understanding of a man whose mind is tranquil quickly becomes firmly settled.
N: Prasāda, the tranquility attained at the end of verse 64, is now shown to cause two further goods: the end of all sorrow, and a buddhi that settles quickly (āśu) — a positive chain of causation answering the negative one of verses 62–63 point for point.
#66
L: There-is-not understanding for-the-undisciplined, and-not for-the-undisciplined [is there] contemplative-power; and-for-one-without-contemplative-power [there is] no peace; for-one-without-peace, whence [could there be] happiness?
I: The undisciplined man has no understanding, and no power of contemplation either; without contemplation there is no peace, and without peace, how can there be happiness?
N: A chain of negatives mirroring, in reverse, the positive chain of verses 64–65: the undisciplined (ayukta) lack buddhi and bhāvanā; without bhāvanā there is no śānti; without śānti no sukha. This closes the sthitaprajña section's argument proper before the final image of the ocean in verse 70.
#67
L: Of-the-senses, indeed, roaming, which mind follows — that carries-off his wisdom, as-wind a-boat on-the-water.
I: When the mind follows the roaming senses, it carries off a man's wisdom, as the wind carries off a boat on the water.
N: A second memorable image, after the tortoise of verse 58: vāyur nāvam ivāmbhasi, 'like wind carrying off a boat on the water' — the mind that trails after the roving senses is as helpless as an unmanned boat in a gale. This restates, in one simile, the whole mechanism of verses 60–63.
#68
L: Therefore, of-whom, O mighty-armed-one, restrained wholly [are] the-senses from-the-objects-of-the-senses — his wisdom [is] firmly-established.
I: Therefore, mighty-armed one, the man whose senses are wholly restrained from their objects — his wisdom is firmly established.
N: A closing restatement of verse 58's tortoise principle in plain terms, without the simile, as the sthitaprajña portrait turns toward its final image (the ocean of verse 70) and conclusion (verses 71–72). Mahābāho, 'mighty-armed one', addressed to Arjuna the warrior, quietly reminds the listener that this teaching on inward restraint is meant for a man about to fight, not a renunciant withdrawing from the world.
#69
L: What [is] night for-all-beings, in-that the-self-controlled-one is-awake; in-which beings are-awake, that [is] night for-the-seeing sage.
I: What is night for all beings, in that the disciplined man is awake; and what all beings are awake to, that is night for the sage who sees.
N: A verse built entirely on a paradoxical reversal of niśā, 'night', and jāgṛ, 'to be awake' — the sthitaprajña is awake to a reality that ordinary beings sleep through, and asleep (uninterested) in the ordinary pursuits that keep them awake. Muni, 'sage', returns from verse 56 to close the portrait's central section with the same word it began with.
#70
L: Being-filled, whose-foundation-is-unmoving, the-ocean, waters enter, just-as; likewise desires whom enter, all — he attains peace, not the-desirer-of-desires.
I: As waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet stays unmoving in its depths, so all desires enter the man who attains peace — not the man who desires desires.
N: The chapter's second great simile for the sthitaprajña, after the tortoise of verse 58: the ocean, into which every river empties without ever overflowing or being disturbed (acala-pratiṣṭham, 'unmoving in its foundation'), receives desires the way it receives rivers — without being moved by them. Kāma-kāmī, 'a desirer of desires' (one who chases wanting itself), is set against the man who has attained śānti; both closing words look back to kāma at the start of the chain in verse 62.
#71
L: Having-abandoned desires, who all, a-man lives free-from-longing; without-mine-ness, without-egoism, he attains peace.
I: The man who abandons all desires and lives free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' or of 'I' — he attains peace.
N: Nirmamaḥ, 'without mine-ness', and nirahaṃkāraḥ, 'without egoism' (literally 'the I-maker'), name the two possessive structures — ownership and selfhood — that the discipline since verse 55 has been dismantling; the verse effectively restates verse 55's definition (ātmani eva ātmanā tuṣṭaḥ) with the emphasis now on what has been let go rather than on what remains.
#72
L: This [is] the-brahman-state, O Pārtha; not-it having-attained, one-is-deluded. Having-remained in-this even at-the-time-of-death, the-beatitude-of-brahman one-reaches.
I: This is the state that is brahman, Pārtha; having attained it, one is no longer deluded. Remaining in it even at the hour of death, one reaches the beatitude of brahman.
N: The chapter's closing verse names the sthitaprajña's condition brāhmī sthitiḥ, 'the brahman-state' — the first appearance of brahman (kept untranslated per convention) in the poem, quietly identifying the steady wisdom described since verse 55 with the highest reality itself, not treating it as merely a psychological achievement. Brahma-nirvāṇam, 'the nirvāṇa that is brahman' (nirvāṇa literally 'blown out', as a flame is extinguished), uses a word later strongly associated with Buddhism in a purely Vedāntic sense here; anta-kāle 'pi, 'even at the moment of death', promises that this state, reached even once at the very end, is enough — closing the chapter's whole argument, which began with Arjuna's fear of death, by placing death itself inside a state that fear can no longer touch.
